metadata.title: Combining Statistical and Machine Learning Methods to Identify Predictors of Brazilian Students’ Proficiency in PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study analyzed PISA 2018 public-use data for Brazil, using the PISA complex survey design (multistage sampling, unequal sampling probabilities, and stratification). The analytic sample was restricted to 15-year-old students and their schools in Brazil, with further splitting into two analysis groups (A1 for random forest and A2 for multilevel logistic regression) and separate multiple-imputation runs for each group. The manuscript does not report applying specific PISA sampling or replicate weights (e.g., student weight variables or BRR/jackknife replicate weights), so it is unclear whether complex-survey weighting was used in the ML and multilevel estimation steps. Because random forests in scikit-learn are typically fit without native survey-weight support, the safest interpretation is that weights were either not applied or not explicitly documented; readers should verify in the supplementary material or original PISA weight documentation before using the odds ratios for population-representative inference.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: PISA proficiency outcomes were dichotomized into “Low Proficiency” vs “Proficient” based on PISA proficiency levels (Level 2 threshold), so the dependent variables are not PV-based continuous achievement scores. As a result, plausible-value handling is not applicable to the modeled outcomes in this paper. Missingness was addressed via multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) to create complete datasets for the two analysis subsamples, but the paper does not describe any PV-specific combining step because the outcome is a proficiency category rather than a PV score.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 public-use files for Brazil, targeting the population of 15-year-old students and their schools. The study then created two analytic subsamples for the two-step pipeline: A1 (random forest) with n=5345 and A2 (multilevel logistic regression) with n=5346. Missing responses were handled by multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) separately within A1 and A2, using all variables included in the analyses. Outcomes were defined by PISA proficiency levels for mathematics, science, and reading, then dichotomized into “Low Proficiency” (below Level 2) and “Proficient” (Level 2 or above).

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (A1): out-of-bag accuracy = 87.2% (95% CI: 87.2%–87.3%); Multilevel logistic regression (A2): AUC-ROC = 92.5% (95% CI: 91.7%–93.3%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics data for Brazil, the study leveraged Annual household income, Metacognition: Summarizing subscale, Metacognition: Assess credibility subscale, Parents’ highest occupational status, and Metacognition: Understanding and remembering subscale to predict Mathematics proficiency (Low vs Proficient), finding that higher household income and parental occupational status were positively associated with proficiency while grade repetition and additional instruction were negatively associated. This indicates that strengthening early childhood education and care and reducing grade repetition may improve baseline mathematics proficiency, while interpreting “additional instruction” as potentially reflecting remedial need rather than causal enrichment.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (A1): out-of-bag accuracy = 86.7% (95% CI: 86.6%–86.8%); Multilevel logistic regression (A2): AUC-ROC = 91.7% (95% CI: 90.9%–92.6%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Science data for Brazil, the study leveraged Metacognition: Assess credibility subscale, Additional instruction, Metacognition: Summarizing subscale, Annual household income, and Metacognition: Understanding and remembering subscale to predict Science proficiency (Low vs Proficient), finding that higher household income and parental occupational status were positively associated with proficiency while grade repetition and additional instruction were negatively associated. This indicates that policies combining socioeconomic support with metacognitive skill development and targeted retention reform may raise science proficiency, though the negative association with additional instruction likely reflects selection into remedial support rather than program effectiveness.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (A1): out-of-bag accuracy = 86.9% (95% CI: 86.8%–87.0%); Multilevel logistic regression (A2): AUC-ROC = 92.8% (95% CI: 92.1%–93.5%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data for Brazil, the study leveraged Metacognition: Assess credibility subscale, Additional instruction, Metacognition: Summarizing subscale, Annual household income, and Metacognition: Understanding and remembering subscale to predict Reading proficiency (Low vs Proficient), finding that higher household income and parental occupational status were positively associated with proficiency while grade repetition and additional instruction were negatively associated. This indicates that strengthening early childhood education and care and supporting students’ metacognitive learning strategies may help move more students into baseline reading proficiency, while cautioning that cross-sectional associations cannot establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study used PISA 2018 public-use data for Brazil (15-year-olds; N=10,691 students across 597 schools) and dichotomized PISA proficiency into “Low Proficiency” vs “Proficient” (Level 2 threshold) for mathematics, science, and reading. A two-step pipeline was applied separately for each domain: a single-level Random Forest classifier (A1) to rank predictors using mean decrease in accuracy (MDA), followed by adjusted multilevel logistic regression (A2) to estimate odds ratios while accounting for students nested within schools. Random-forest out-of-bag accuracy was 87.2% (math), 86.7% (science), and 86.9% (reading), and multilevel models achieved AUC-ROC of 92.5%, 91.7%, and 92.8%, respectively. Across domains, top predictors included annual household income, parents’ occupational status, early childhood education and care, metacognition subscales, and additional instruction; grade repetition was consistently negative. Limitations include cross-sectional design, self-report measures, and multiple imputation for missingness; the paper does not explicitly document the use of PISA sampling/replicate weights, which may affect population-representative inference.
